---
title: Input distributions
description: "Inspect field distributions across training, validation, test, and prediction, and configure drift warnings."
---

A different validation or prediction population can be intentional: customers,
markets, and calendar periods change. relflow records bounded input distribution
metadata and warns about large differences from training. The warning identifies
what changed; the application decides whether that change is expected.

## Enable monitoring

Monitoring is **off by default**. Set `drift=True` on `Model` or any model preset
such as `Model.xs` to enable it for that model. When disabled, encoding skips
profile construction and the model skips drift comparisons for every field,
even if a field declares a custom `Drift` policy.

After opting in, set a field's `drift` policy to change its tolerance, or use
`drift=False` to exclude that field:

```python
import relflow as rf

model = rf.Model.xs(
    drift=True,
    amount=rf.Number(drift=rf.Drift(threshold=0.3, min_samples=256)),
    merchant=rf.Category,
    payment_id=rf.Hash(drift=False),
    disputed=rf.Boolean(mask=True),
)
```

The same `drift: true` option is accepted in a YAML model template. You can also
set `model.drift = True` before using an existing model. Select the setting before
creating data loaders; loaders capture it for their encoding workers. Disabling
`model.drift` stops model-side updates and comparisons while retaining existing
profiles. Recreate loaders to change their worker-side profiling policy.

Training supplies the reference. Validation, test, and prediction supply separate
comparison profiles. Inputs are observed after preprocessing, explicit queries,
and collection cropping, before masking or jitter. Padding is excluded. Profiles
include targets during training, validation, and testing. Prediction omits
fields that are never embedded, such as the supervised `disputed` target above;
missing answers are expected there.

The same monitoring applies to direct `model.encode(...)`, direct
`model.predict(...)`, and Arrow data module batches consumed by model loops.
Workers carry bounded summaries to the model; they do not update the metadata
or learned resources. Raw tensor-only forward calls have no pristine input
metadata and do not contribute profiles. Lightning sanity checks are excluded.

## Inspect metadata

After consuming inputs, obtain JSON-compatible metadata:

```python
metadata = model.distributions.summary()
training_amount = metadata["/amount"]["train"]["value"]
# Keys: count, quantiles. Quantiles represent minimum, 25%, median, 75%, maximum.
```

The metadata lives on the model independently of its learned normalizers and
vocabularies. Evaluation cannot update the training reference or train the
model. Checkpoints retain the model-wide `drift` setting, distribution profiles, and
warning suppression. Older checkpoints that lack the setting load with
monitoring disabled. Schema changes discard profiles
whose field or ancestor configuration changed. This diagnostic metadata does
not appear in prediction output tables.

Profiles accumulate across batches and calls, including repeated epochs. A new
comparison window can retain the training reference:

```python
model.distributions.clear(strata="predict")
model.distributions.clear(address="/merchant", strata="validate")
```

Call `model.distributions.clear()` to start over, including the training
reference. Clearing a reference or comparison also rearms the relevant warnings.
Within a window, each field, comparison stratum, and feature logs at most once.

## What is measured

| Field | Features |
|---|---|
| Every active field after model opt-in | Structural value/null/other state frequencies, excluding padding |
| `Number`, `Quantile` | Finite source-value distribution; separate finite, NaN, positive-infinity, and negative-infinity frequencies |
| `Duration`, `Ordinal` | Numeric profiles of derived elapsed values or ranks, after their source queries and declarations are applied |
| `Boolean` | False/true frequencies |
| `Category`, `Enum`, `Group`, `Hash` | Label frequencies in 128 fixed identity buckets |
| `Set` | Deduplicated member frequencies and set size, after label folding and dropping null/NaN members |
| `Text` | Character length, without running its encoder |
| `Vector` | Component mean, vector norm, and finite-vector frequency |
| `Period` / `DateParts` | Sine and cosine distributions of each configured calendar part |

Label folding follows `strip` and `cased` options. Identity buckets retain no
raw labels and never grow a vocabulary. Hash field profiling uses fixed identity
buckets independently of its training salts. Bucket metadata records the Polars
version that defines its hash encoding; a changed encoding discards the affected
feature profiles and starts collecting a new reference. Numeric features use bounded
merging digests, without retaining observation history. State frequencies
refer to the Arrow structural states; extension-specific nonfinite features
separately describe numerical validity.

## How warnings work

The numeric distance approximates the largest difference between the two
cumulative distributions, so it can detect location, spread, and shape changes.
Categorical distance is total variation over the fixed histogram. Both distances
range from zero to one. A feature must have at least `min_samples` observations
in both training and comparison before it can warn; finite numeric observations
and set members have their own counts.

A warning requires a distance larger than `threshold` plus an allowance for
finite sample noise. The allowance grows with occupied categorical buckets and
shrinks as counts increase. Logs include the field address, feature, stratum,
reference and observed counts, distance, threshold, allowance, and rank. The
threshold is a diagnostic tolerance, not a significance level or a guaranteed
false-positive rate. Increase it when that field's population is expected to
change, or disable that field's monitor.

These are marginal diagnostics. They can miss changes to relationships among
fields, label collisions in identity buckets, semantic text changes, vector
changes that preserve mean and norm, and rare events. Cumulative windows can
hide recent changes; clear the comparison profile for a fresh window. Profiles
under distributed execution are **rank-local**, with no extra collectives or
global distribution claim. Their reference counts describe observed exposures,
not necessarily unique source rows. Warning suppression persists until cleared,
even when a subsequent change affects the same feature.

## Custom tensorfields

An extension can register `rf.Component.profile` with a callable accepting a
pristine `rf.RaggedField` and keyword `request`. Return a mapping from stable
feature names to `rf.Distribution` objects. For example, a numeric custom field
can expose a source-value distribution:

```python
@extension.register(rf.Component.profile)
def profile(field, *, request):
    return {"value": rf.Distribution.numeric(field.values)}
```

Use `rf.Distribution.categorical(indices, bins=N)` for a fixed histogram, where
`indices` is a one-dimensional NumPy integer array in `[0, N)`. The extension
owns feature meaning and preprocessing; the shared path merges and compares
summaries. The feature name `state` is reserved for structural profiling.
Extensions without this component still receive structural state monitoring.


## Controlled research studies

The optional studies [Numeric shifts](../evidence/distributions/numeric-shifts.py),
[Typed shifts](../evidence/distributions/typed-shifts.py), and
[Policies and checkpoints](../evidence/distributions/policies-and-checkpoints.py)
predeclare three-seed detection checks and quiet controls for the unreleased
monitoring wheel. Local lab records are separate from published measurements;
these studies do not replace the complete paired core gate.


The [Enum](../evidence/distributions/enum-shifts.py),
[Hash](../evidence/distributions/hash-shifts.py), and
[Group](../evidence/distributions/group-shifts.py) studies extend detection
and quiet-control checks across validation, test, and prediction. They also
check incremental batch accumulation, minimum sample counts, and warning
suppression. Enum checks undeclared-label rejection, Hash separates profiling
from training salts, and Group checks that evaluation leaves its vocabulary
and learned assignments unchanged.
